{{Short description|Operator in quantum physics}}
In [[quantum physics]], the '''squeeze operator''' for a single mode of the electromagnetic field is<ref>{{cite book
 |title=Introductory quantum optics
 |author1=Gerry, C.C.  |author2=Knight, P.L.
  |name-list-style=amp |isbn=978-0-521-52735-4
 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=CgByyoBJJwgC&pg=PA182
 |year=2005
 |publisher=Cambridge University Press
 |page=182}}</ref>

:<math>\hat{S}(z) = \exp \left ( {1 \over 2} (z^* \hat{a}^2 - z \hat{a}^{\dagger 2}) \right ) , \qquad z = r \, e^{i\theta}</math>

where the [[Operator (mathematics)|operators]] inside the [[Exponential function|exponential]] are the [[ladder operators]].  It is a unitary operator and therefore obeys <math>S(z)\,S^\dagger (z) = S^\dagger (z)\,S(z) = \hat 1</math>, where <math>\hat 1</math> is the identity operator.

Its action on the annihilation and creation operators produces

:<math>\hat{S}^{\dagger}(z) \, \hat{a} \, \hat{S}(z) = \hat{a}\cosh r - e^{i\theta} \hat{a}^{\dagger} \sinh r  \qquad\text{and}\qquad \hat{S}^{\dagger}(z) \, \hat{a}^{\dagger} \, \hat{S}(z) = \hat{a}^{\dagger}\cosh r - e^{-i\theta} \hat{a} \sinh r </math>

The squeeze operator is ubiquitous in [[quantum optics]] and can operate on any state.  For example, when acting upon the vacuum, the squeezing operator produces the squeezed vacuum state.

The squeezing operator can also act on [[coherent states]] and produce [[squeezed coherent states]]. The squeezing operator does not commute with the [[displacement operator]]:

: <math>\hat{S}(z) \hat{D}(\alpha) \neq \hat{D}(\alpha) \hat{S}(z),</math>

nor does it commute with the ladder operators, so one must pay close attention to how the operators are used. There is, however, a simple braiding relation, 
<math> \hat{D}(\alpha)\hat{S}(z) =\hat{S}(z)\hat{S}^{\dagger}(z)\hat{D}(\alpha)\hat{S}(z)= \hat{S}(z)\hat{D}(\gamma), \qquad\text{where}\qquad \gamma=\alpha\cosh r + \alpha^* e^{i\theta} \sinh r </math><ref>M. M. Nieto and D. Truax (1995), {{cite journal|title=Holstein-Primakoff/Bogoliubov Transformations and the Multiboson System|year=1997 |doi=10.1002/prop.2190450204|arxiv=quant-ph/9506025|last1=Nieto |first1=Michael Martin |last2=Truax |first2=D. Rodney |journal=Fortschritte der Physik/Progress of Physics |volume=45 |issue=2 |pages=145–156 |bibcode=1997ForPh..45..145N |s2cid=14213781 }} Eqn (15). Note that in this reference, the definition of the squeeze operator (eqn. 12) differs by a minus sign inside the exponential, therefore the expression of <math>\gamma</math> is modified accordingly (<math>\theta \rightarrow \theta+\pi</math>).</ref>

Application of both operators above on the vacuum produces a displaced squeezed state:

:<math>\hat{D}(\alpha)\hat{S}(r)|0\rangle=|r, \alpha\rangle</math>.

Or a [[squeezed coherent state]]:

:<math>\hat{S}(r)\hat{D}(\alpha)|0\rangle=|\alpha,r\rangle</math>.

== Derivation of action on creation operator ==
As mentioned above, the action of the squeeze operator <math>S(z)</math> on the annihilation operator <math>a</math> can be written as <math display="block">S^\dagger(z) a S(z)=\cosh(|z|)a-\frac{z}{|z|}\sinh(|z|)a^\dagger.</math> To derive this equality, let us define the (skew-Hermitian) operator <math>A\equiv (z a^{\dagger 2}-z^* a^2)/2</math>, so that <math>S^\dagger =e^A</math>.

The left hand side of the equality is thus <math>e^A a e^{-A}</math>. We can now make use of the [[Baker–Campbell–Hausdorff formula#An important lemma and its application to a special case of the Baker–Campbell–Hausdorff formula|general equality]] <math display="block">e^A B e^{-A}=\sum_{k=0}^\infty \frac{1}{k!}[\underbrace{A,[A,\dots,[A}_{k\,\text{times}},B]\dots]],</math> which holds true for any pair of operators <math>A</math> and <math>B</math>. To compute <math>e^A a e^{-A}</math> thus reduces to the problem of computing the repeated commutators between <math>A</math> and <math>a</math>.
As can be readily verified, we have<math display="block">[A,a]=\frac{1}{2}[z a^{\dagger 2}-z^* a^2,a]
= \frac{z}{2}[a^{\dagger 2},a] = -z a^\dagger,</math><math display="block">[A,a^\dagger]=\frac{1}{2}[z a^{\dagger 2}-z^* a^2,a^\dagger]
= -\frac{z^*}{2}[a^{2},a^\dagger] = -z^* a.</math>Using these equalities, we obtain

<math>[\underbrace{A,[A,\dots,[A}_{k},a]\dots]]=
\begin{cases}
    |z|^k a, & \text{ for }k\text{ even},\\
    -z|z|^{k-1} a^\dagger, & \text{ for }k\text{ odd}.
\end{cases}</math>

so that finally we get

<math>e^A a e^{-A}=
a \sum_{k=0}^\infty \frac{|z|^{2k}}{(2k)!}
- a^\dagger \frac{z}{|z|}\sum_{k=0}^\infty \frac{|z|^{2k+1}}{(2k+1)!}
= a\cosh|z|- a^\dagger e^{i\theta}\sinh|z|.</math>

The same result is also obtained by differentiating the transformed operator

:<math>
a(t) = e^{tA} a \, e^{-tA}
</math>
with respect to the parameter <math>t</math>. A linear system of differential equations for <math>a(t)</math> and <math>a^\dagger(t)</math> emerges when working through the commutators <math>[A, a(t)]</math> and <math>[A, a^\dagger(t)]</math>. Their formal solution provides the transformed operator <math>\hat{S}^\dagger a\,\hat{S} = a(t=1)</math> as linear combination of <math>a</math> and <math>a^\dagger</math>. The technique can be generalised to other operators or state transformations.<ref>{{cite journal|title=Exponential Operators and Parameter Differentiation in Quantum Physics | first1=R. M. | last1=Wilcox | journal=J. Math. Phys. | volume=8 | issue=4 | year=1967 | pages=962–82 | doi=10.1063/1.1705306| bibcode=1967JMP.....8..962W }}</ref>
